title: Najdorf: model games
outcomes: Predicts the next move at twelve decision points in three real Najdorf games and names the turning point of each, with the engine's evaluation
Explains in a sentence per phase what each side is doing in the English Attack race, in a quiet Be2 game and in the poisoned-pawn line
Tells a game result from an evaluation: Caruana's non-engine Be2 won, Nakamura's ...Bd6 opponent lost, Anand's equal-looking position lost
Reads our master counts (with sample sizes) after 6.Be3 e6, 6.Be2 e5 and 8.Qd2, and says what they do not show
sources: library/data/games (TWIC weekly PGN zips, 2012 to 2026): the 4,389 games found by script in which both players are rated 2550+ and the first ten plies are 1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 d6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 a6; three classical games chosen by hand, their moves and results checked with python-chess [V]. Game 1: Bok - Gordievsky, 80th Tata Steel Group B, Wijk aan Zee, 24 Jan 2018, 0-1. Game 2: Anand - Vachier-Lagrave, 7th London Classic, London, 11 Dec 2015, 0-1. Game 3: Caruana - Vachier-Lagrave, 83rd Tata Steel Masters, Wijk aan Zee, 23 Jan 2021, 1-0. Nakamura - Grandelius, Gibraltar Masters, 26 Jan 2018, 1-0, is used for its 14th move only. Moves and results are facts; every comment is our own wording

steps.text: **The question.** What decides a real Najdorf game: the opening, or what happens after it? You will play through three games between players rated above 2,550, predict the decision points and see what the engine says at each. A warning about the word *model*: I picked three games with clear stories from the 4,389 games with both players rated 2,550 or more in our files. They are examples, not a sample of how Najdorfs usually end [V].

**Game 1: the English Attack race.** White (Bok) plays Be3, f3, Qd2 and long castling; Black (Gordievsky) answers with ...e6 and ...b5. The kings will stand on opposite wings, so each side can throw pawns at the enemy king. In our masters file White played f3 in 134 of 385 games after 6.Be3 e6, and Black chose ...b5 in 146 of the 186 that went on [S: stats.json, 2,500+ players, includes rapid and blitz]. Step through the first moves.

steps.text: **The central strike.** When an opponent attacks on a wing, a blow in the centre is often the answer [H]. Black's ...d5 needed three things: the bishop already on the long diagonal, the e4 pawn lightly held, and White's king far from the centre. Remove one and the strike changes. The same position arose in two games two days apart. Compare the next move.

Nakamura won that game; Bok lost his. The engine (depth 16) puts ...dxe4 and ...e5 both within a third of a pawn of the best, and ...Bd6 clearly behind. A result is not an evaluation. steps.text: **What decided game 1.** Not the opening. From move 6 to move 16 the engine put White between about +0.3 and +0.9 (depth 16, one run [V]). Black found the best defence, the ...d5 strike, but White kept about half a pawn until move 17. Then two slips ended it: Rhe1 (nearly a pawn) and Nd3 (nearly three pawns) [V]. [I] The strike in the centre worked because White's king was far from the centre.

In a game like this small things decide.

steps.text: **What decided game 2.** The position was level at move 23 [V]; one queen move then lost the game. The mistake did not come from the opening or from a bad plan: it came from not checking what was attacked. [H] In quiet structures a slip usually happens on a square that has more attackers than defenders. Ask: which of my pieces is already loose or overloaded?

**Game 3: the poisoned pawn.** In the Bg5 Najdorf Black plays ...Qb6 and, after Qd2, takes the b2 pawn. In 162 master games with 8.Qd2, Black took in 149: White won 26, 104 were drawn, Black won 19 [S: stats.json]. White scored 52%, Black 48%. Taking is playable, which is why strong players have chosen it for decades. Caruana (White) and Vachier-Lagrave (Black) played it in January 2021.

steps.text: **What decided game 3.** Not the poisoned pawn: the engine rates the position after the capture as roughly equal [V]. White left the engine's first choice with 10.Be2 (about 0.6 pawn behind f5); Black's ...Nc6 was within 0.2 of the best, and the game stayed balanced until Black's recapture on d5. One recapture decided it: ...exd5 instead of ...cxd5 [V]. [I] The structure after the capture mattered more than the pawn. White then converted over twenty more moves.

**Three games, three decisions.** Game 1 turned on two slips after Black found the best defence; game 2 on one queen move after a balanced middlegame; game 3 on one recapture. [H] In all three, the swing came within a few moves of a forcing line and the opening itself did not decide. That may be true only of the games I picked: a larger sample would test it. The next lesson looks at a scan of 250 decisive games [S: counts not re-run here].

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- Game 1: the English Attack race; ...d5 was the best defence; two slips ended it.
- Game 2: the quiet game; level at move 23; one queen move.
- Game 3: the poisoned pawn; playable; the recapture decided.
- [V] Engine claims at depth 16; [S] counts from our masters file (2,500+ players, 2012 to 2026, rapid and blitz included).
- [H] Small errors near forcing lines decide more games than the opening choice; untested beyond these three games.
